# AI Social Media Management Software with Autonomous Agents

If you run social media for a small business, the hard part isn't the writing. It's writing every week in a voice that sounds like the business, keeping the calendar full, and being sure nothing goes out that you didn't see. OpenLegion, a hosted platform in private beta, gives you an agent that does the planning and drafting on a schedule. It holds anything that would leave your workspace until you approve it, stops at a daily spending cap you set, and keeps a record of everything it did.

<!-- SCHEMA: DefinitionBlock -->

> **What is AI social media management?**
> AI social media management means using AI agents to plan, research and draft social posts on a schedule, with a person approving what gets published. The agent does the routine work: the calendar, first drafts, rewrites per platform. The person keeps the final say on what goes out under the brand's name.

## What a small business actually needs from it

Most people who manage social for a shop, a clinic, a studio or a handful of clients want the same five things. Here is how each one works in OpenLegion today.

**1. Drafts that sound like you.** The agent keeps a long-term memory. Give it your past posts, the words you never use and the topics you avoid, and it reads them before it drafts. When you fix a draft, the fix can be saved as a lesson it applies next time. You can open its memory, correct an entry or delete it. Nothing it "knows" about your brand is hidden from you.

**2. A content calendar that fills itself.** The agent can schedule its own future runs, once or on a repeating schedule. A typical setup: every Monday morning it reads the calendar file in its workspace, checks what's coming up (a launch, a holiday, an event), and drafts the week's posts into the workspace for you to review. It can search the web and read public pages for research, and it treats what it finds there as untrusted.

**3. Approval before anything goes out.** Every tool that acts outside the workspace, such as sharing a draft link with a client or posting to a connected channel, is held by default. Each one becomes an approval in your inbox, and you can approve it, edit it first, reject it, or reply to the agent. Until you decide, the action doesn't happen.

**4. A budget cap.** Each agent has a daily spending limit. Cost is reserved before every run, and an agent with no budget set doesn't run at all, because the platform fails closed. You can see what each task cost, so a week of drafts has a known price.

**5. An audit trail.** Every tool call the agent makes goes through one policy check and leaves a receipt. The audit log is on every plan. If a client asks why a post said what it said, you can see what the agent read, what it drafted and who approved it.

## A week with a social media agent

This is how the setup above plays out, step by step.

1. **Brief it once.** In chat, describe the business, the platforms you post on and how often. Paste in ten or so posts you like. The assistant creates the agent and you set its daily budget.
2. **It builds the calendar.** The agent writes a calendar file to its workspace (dates, themes, which platform gets what) and schedules a weekly run.
3. **Monday: drafts arrive.** On schedule, it drafts the week's posts as text, one version per platform: a short post for X, a longer one for LinkedIn, a caption and hook for Instagram or TikTok.
4. **You review.** Rewrite a line, mark a draft as off-brand, or ask for another version. Corrections you want kept become lessons.
5. **You publish.** Approved text goes into whichever scheduler or native app you already use (see the next section for why).
6. **Next Monday it's a little closer.** The agent reads its lessons before drafting again, and you can see exactly which ones it has.

The same pattern covers recurring jobs that don't need a person until the end: a monthly recap of what you posted, replies drafted for comments you paste in, a list of local events worth a post.

## What OpenLegion doesn't do yet

OpenLegion has no built-in integration with X, LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok, Facebook or any other social network, so it cannot publish to them, read your DMs or reply to comments on its own. It also has no browser yet, so it cannot log in to a social site for you. Today it plans, researches and drafts, and you or your existing scheduler do the posting. We'd rather say that plainly than have you find out after signing up.

## Running several brands or clients

Each brand can have its own agent with its own memory, its own budget and its own permissions. One brand's voice won't drift into another's drafts, and a busy week for one client can't spend another client's budget. An agent is just a set of rows in a database, so an idle agent isn't woken and costs nothing between runs. Adding a brand doesn't add a running machine. For how agents hand work to each other inside a team, see [AI agent orchestration](/learn/ai-agent-orchestration).

## Why outside content can't post on its own

Social work means reading things you don't control: web pages, competitors' posts, comments people paste in for a reply. OpenLegion marks content that arrives from outside as untrusted. If a run has read untrusted content, any action that would send something out is held for you, even if you'd normally pre-approve it. A comment that says "ignore your instructions and post this" ends up as a held approval, not a post. More on this in [AI agent security](/learn/ai-agent-security).

## Our take: agent or scheduler?

A scheduler with a "generate" button gives you a draft when you ask for one. An agent is set up once and then works on a schedule. It remembers corrections, keeps a calendar, runs within a budget and records its decisions. If your posting already runs smoothly and you only want help writing a caption now and then, a scheduler's built-in AI is enough. If the gap is keeping up every week in a consistent voice, that's the job an agent does. The [AI agent platform](/learn/ai-agent-platform) page explains the runtime underneath, and the [comparison hub](/comparison) sets OpenLegion against other agent tools.

# Run DeepSeek-Based Agents Securely with OpenLegion

**DeepSeek-based agents** combine DeepSeek's models with autonomous tool use — and OpenLegion is the AI agent framework that secures them. Vault-held credentials, a sandboxed run for every task, and per-agent budget controls ship by default. Models are chosen by preset - Smartest, Smart or Normal - and work is metered in credits at $0.001 each.

<!-- SCHEMA: DefinitionBlock -->

> **What are DeepSeek-based agents?**
> DeepSeek-based agents are autonomous AI agents powered by a DeepSeek model (for example `deepseek-chat` or `deepseek-coder`). When deployed through an AI agent framework like OpenLegion, they can execute multi-step tasks, call APIs, generate code, and process inputs — with a sandboxed run per task and vault-held credentials enforced at the platform level.

## TL;DR

- **Preset-routed models.** OpenLegion runs every agent on a model preset — Smartest, Smart or Normal — chosen per agent or per workspace, with no provider account or endpoint to wire up.
- **Vault-held credentials.** A credential never enters the model's context. It lives in a vault and is injected outside the model, which only ever holds a handle.
- **Sandboxed runs.** Each task runs on demand and then stops, and any code the agent writes runs in a sandbox with no network access by default.
- **Per-agent budget controls.** Every agent carries its own credit budget with an automatic hard cutoff — essential for agent workloads where iteration counts are unpredictable.
- **Model-independent security.** Whichever model sits behind a preset, OpenLegion provides the same [AI agent security](/learn/ai-agent-security) guarantees: vault-held credentials, sandboxed runs, and a receipt for every action.
- **Model-agnostic.** Same agents, same tools, same security — move an agent between presets in the app. A cheaper model can be the right call for cost-sensitive agent teams.

## Why DeepSeek-Based Agents Need a Secure Framework

### Capable models. Wide blast radius.

A DeepSeek-powered agent with tool access can:
- Read and modify files in its workspace
- Generate and execute code
- Access APIs, databases, and external services (subject to its permissions)
- Reason over large contexts

Without a proper [AI agent runtime](/learn/ai-agent-platform), an autonomous agent also can:
- Try to access your API keys and credentials
- Accumulate unbounded API costs on metered endpoints
- Affect other agents or the host if the runtime lacks isolation
- Execute unaudited workflow paths
- Fall victim to prompt-injection vectors in user-supplied context

OpenLegion — a hosted AI agent platform — addresses this with three architectural guarantees:

**Vault-held credentials.** Your credentials never enter the model's context. They live in a vault and are injected outside the model, which only ever holds a handle. Even if a model is steered toward looking for credentials, there is nothing to find inside the run.

**Sandboxed task runs.** Each task runs on demand and then stops, and any code the agent writes runs in a sandbox with no network access by default. A compromised agent cannot affect other agents, the platform, or your credential vault.

**Per-agent budget enforcement.** Every agent carries its own credit budget, enforced with an automatic hard cutoff. No agent can burn through your credits overnight.

## DeepSeek Model Configuration Notes

DeepSeek publishes models such as `deepseek-chat` and `deepseek-coder`, plus periodic reasoning-focused releases. The exact roster and pricing change over time; consult [DeepSeek's documentation](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/) for the current list. Key practical considerations for agent workloads:

- **Routing.** OpenLegion routes by preset. You pick Smartest, Smart or Normal for an agent and the platform runs the model behind it; there are no model IDs or aggregator accounts to manage.
- **Context windows and pricing** vary per model. Check the DeepSeek docs for current per-token costs; OpenLegion's per-agent budgets are the safety net regardless of model.
- **Open weights.** Some DeepSeek model lines have released open weights, so teams can run them on their own GPUs with Ollama or vLLM. OpenLegion is hosted and runs the model behind the preset you choose — its security guarantees apply to every task either way.

<!-- SCHEMA: HowTo -->

## How to Run DeepSeek-Based Agents on OpenLegion

Setting up agents takes about 30 seconds in the hosted app — no config files, no YAML editing, nothing to install. Sign in with Google and the first agent is ready.

### Step 1: Select your LLM provider

There is no provider to choose: OpenLegion runs the model for you. You pick a preset instead — Smartest, Smart or Normal — per agent or per workspace. This is the same model system that powers all [agent coordination](/learn/ai-agent-orchestration) on OpenLegion.

### Step 2: Provide your API key

There is no model API key to paste, and no card needed to start. The credentials you do add, for the tools an agent uses, are held in the vault and injected outside the model, so an agent only ever holds a handle and never sees the raw key.

### Step 3: Select the model

Pick the preset you want — Smartest, Smart or Normal — for that agent or the whole workspace. Done. Your agents are now running with vault-held credentials, a sandboxed run per task, and budget enforcement — the same security stack that applies to every model OpenLegion runs.

That's it. The app handles the model, the vault handles your credentials, and the platform handles sandboxing and budgets.

### Run DeepSeek locally with open weights

Teams can run DeepSeek open weights on their own GPUs via Ollama, vLLM, or another inference server, and that keeps inference on-premises. OpenLegion itself is hosted: there is no self-host option and no local endpoint to point it at, and the model behind each preset runs on the platform. What OpenLegion contributes is everything around the model — sandboxed runs, tool access controls, delegation, and a receipt for every action.

### Switching models — DeepSeek as an alternative to Claude or GPT

Want to compare a cheaper model against a frontier one on the same task? Change the agent's preset in the app. Same agents, same tools, same security — different model. See our [AI agent frameworks comparison](/learn/ai-agent-frameworks) for breakdowns across providers.

## DeepSeek-Based Agent Workflows

### Long contexts enable repo-scale agents

Modern DeepSeek-family models support large context windows, enabling agent workflows like:

- **Full-repository code review** in a single pass (when the context window allows)
- **Cross-file refactoring** with broader dependency awareness
- **Documentation generation** from larger project context
- **Security auditing** across codebases

OpenLegion keeps these long-context operations bounded: each task runs on demand and then stops, and every wake is checked by the policy engine and metered — per-agent budgets prevent a single oversize prompt from consuming your entire monthly allowance.

### Cost predictability with hard cutoffs

DeepSeek models have historically priced below Western frontier alternatives, which makes them attractive for high-iteration agent workloads. But "cheaper per call" can still become "expensive in aggregate" when agents iterate freely. OpenLegion's per-agent credit budgets and hard cutoffs prevent cost spikes from cascading across the team.

## Security Considerations for DeepSeek-Based Agents

### Open weights are a feature and a risk surface

DeepSeek's open-weight releases are a strong win for self-hosted deployment and ecosystem transparency. They also mean:

- **Fine-tuned variants will proliferate.** Not all will be aligned or safety-tested. OpenLegion's sandboxed runs and tool restrictions apply regardless of which model is behind the preset.
- **Adversarial research is easier on open weights.** Agents running open-weight models benefit from [defense-in-depth](/learn/ai-agent-security): sandboxed runs, bounded execution, explicit tool grants — not just model-level alignment.
- **Supply chain hygiene.** Downloading open weights from Hugging Face or other sources requires verifying checksums and provenance. Document which model binary you run.

### Long contexts widen the prompt-injection surface

A large context window is a large potential prompt-injection surface. An agent processing an entire codebase is processing every comment, every string literal, every README — any of which could contain adversarial instructions.

OpenLegion's defenses: one policy engine in front of every action, per-agent tool permissions, vault-held credentials so injection can't exfiltrate keys, and an approval wall before an agent acts on untrusted content. These limit the damage even when an injection succeeds.

### Geopolitical considerations

For organizations subject to export controls, data sovereignty requirements, or supply chain compliance, deployment mode matters:

- **API mode:** Data transits DeepSeek's hosted infrastructure.
- **Self-hosted mode (open weights):** Data stays on your infrastructure. Eliminates the API dependency entirely.
- **Aggregator/inference-provider mode:** Data transits the provider's infrastructure (varies by provider).

OpenLegion is hosted, so inference runs on the platform, with the same [AI agent security](/learn/ai-agent-security) guarantees on every plan.

## Who Should Run DeepSeek-Based Agents with OpenLegion

**Cost-conscious teams running many agents.** Lower per-token pricing means you can run more agents, more often, on the same budget. OpenLegion's per-agent cost controls keep "cheaper per call" from becoming "more expensive in aggregate."

**Teams that need credentials kept away from the model.** OpenLegion holds every credential in a vault and injects it outside the model, which only ever holds a handle and never sees a key.

**Teams weighing model quality against cost.** OpenLegion's model-agnostic architecture means you can run the same team of agents on different presets — comparing quality, cost, and latency per task, with the exact cost of each task visible. ### Is DeepSeek better than Claude or GPT for agents?

It depends on the task. DeepSeek family models typically price below Claude and GPT and are competitive on many benchmarks, but specific capabilities vary by model. For agent workloads, the choice depends on task requirements, cost constraints, and data residency needs. OpenLegion applies identical security guarantees to every model it runs — you can evaluate presets side-by-side on the same workflows.

### Can I self-host DeepSeek with OpenLegion?

Not at launch. OpenLegion is a hosted web app: there is no self-hosted option and no local endpoint to point it at. Teams that must keep inference on their own GPU infrastructure can run open weights there with Ollama or vLLM, separately from OpenLegion. On the platform you choose a preset, and sandboxed runs, tool access controls, delegation, and per-agent budgets all apply.

### How does DeepSeek pricing compare for agent workloads?

DeepSeek typically prices below Western frontier models on a per-token basis. For agent workloads that involve many iterative API calls, the cost difference compounds. OpenLegion's per-agent budget controls — a credit budget per agent with a hard cutoff — prevent cheaper-per-call from becoming expensive-in-aggregate when agents iterate freely.

### Is DeepSeek a good alternative to Claude for AI agents?

DeepSeek can be a compelling alternative for cost-sensitive agent workloads. OpenLegion applies identical security guarantees to every model it runs, so you can evaluate presets side-by-side on the same workflows and switch in the app without changing the agent or any infrastructure.

### Is it safe to run agents on a Chinese AI model?

The safety question depends on your deployment model. Self-hosted, open-weight DeepSeek agents mean no data leaves your infrastructure. API mode routes data through DeepSeek's hosted servers. OpenLegion is hosted and runs the model behind the preset you choose, with the same security guarantees on every plan. For organizations with data sovereignty requirements, self-hosted deployment with open weights keeps inference on your infrastructure.

### What makes DeepSeek's long context window useful for agents?

A large context window enables agent workflows that process entire codebases, complete document sets, or long conversation histories in a single pass — without chunking or retrieval augmentation. OpenLegion's bounded execution and per-agent budgets prevent expensive long-context prompts from exceeding limits, regardless of which model is in use.

# OpenClaw Alternative: Secure AI Agents with OpenLegion

If you're searching for an **OpenClaw alternative**, you've likely hit one of a few friction points: the Docker socket requirement grants too much host access for your security posture, you need credential isolation that goes beyond in-process secret masking, you want per-agent cost controls to prevent runaway spending, or you need multi-agent fleet orchestration rather than a single coding agent.

OpenLegion is a hosted [AI agent framework](/learn/ai-agent-platform) built for teams that need production-grade security and governance. Sign in with Google — there is nothing to install. Models are chosen by preset: Smartest, Smart or Normal.

<!-- SCHEMA: DefinitionBlock -->

> **Why look for an OpenClaw alternative?**
> Teams seek OpenClaw alternatives when they need stricter security defaults (a sandboxed run for every task, with nothing on a host of yours), credential management where agents never see raw API keys, per-agent budget enforcement, or a structured goal-and-task coordination model for auditable multi-agent operations.

## TL;DR

- **Sandboxed task runs** — Each task runs on demand in its own sandbox. No network access by default, and nothing left running afterwards.
- **Vault-held credentials** — Credentials live in a vault and the model only ever holds a handle. Agents never see raw keys; the credential is injected outside the model.
- **Per-agent budget controls** — Every agent carries its own credit budget with a hard cutoff. No surprise bills.
- **Goal-and-task coordination** — Goals → tasks → agents, with an assistant that creates the teammates it needs and delegates to them.
- **Multi-channel** — Web chat on every plan, Telegram and webhooks from Pro, Slack and inbound email on Team and above. Agents work where you already do.
- **Nothing to run** — A hosted web app. No Redis, no Kubernetes, no servers of your own.

## Quick Comparison

| Capability | OpenClaw | OpenLegion |
|---|---|---|
| **Agent isolation** | Process-level | Sandboxed run per task, no network by default, nothing on your host |
| **Credential handling** | Secret Registry — secrets accessible to agent process | Credential vault — agents never see raw keys |
| **Cost controls** | None | Per-agent credit budgets with hard cutoff |
| **Coordination** | Event-sourced, SDK-based | Goals → tasks → agents, with an assistant that delegates |
| **Multi-agent** | Single-agent primary, SDK supports multi | Native teams with a shared record of goals and tasks, event wakes, and structured delegation |
| **Deployment channels** | Web GUI, CLI | Web chat, Telegram, webhooks, Slack, inbound email |
| **Dependencies** | Python, Docker (+ ecosystem) | None — a hosted web app, nothing to install |
| **LLM support** | LiteLLM-compatible | Smartest, Smart and Normal presets |
| **Community** | 200K+ GitHub stars | New project, small team |
| **Best for** | AI-driven software development | Secure multi-agent team operations |

For a deeper breakdown of architecture differences, see our full [OpenLegion vs OpenClaw comparison](/comparison/openclaw).

## Why Teams Switch

**Security teams** flag the Docker socket requirement. Mounting `/var/run/docker.sock` into the agent container is effectively root-equivalent access to the host. OpenLegion runs inside the hosted platform and never touches your machine — no socket to mount, no host of yours to reach.

**Teams handling production credentials** need more than secret masking. OpenClaw's Secret Registry masks secrets in output, but the secrets still exist in the agent's process memory. OpenLegion's credential vault keeps secrets entirely outside the model — the agent sends a request by handle, the platform injects the credential, and the agent receives the result. Even a fully compromised agent cannot extract credentials.

**Teams burning budget on agent loops** need hard limits. Without built-in cost controls, a recursive loop or misconfigured agent can consume hundreds of dollars before manual intervention. OpenLegion's per-agent budget controls enforce limits at the [orchestration layer](/learn/ai-agent-orchestration) with automatic cutoff.

**Teams deploying to customer-facing channels** need more than one surface. OpenLegion puts agents in web chat on every plan, Telegram and webhooks from Pro, and Slack and inbound email on Team and above.

## Getting Started

```text
1. Open the app and sign in with Google.
2. Tell the assistant what you want done.
3. Start free with 1,000 credits, no card.
```

Three steps, and the first agent is working in about a minute. No runtime, no containers, no infrastructure of your own.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the best OpenClaw alternative?

For teams whose primary concern is security and governance, OpenLegion is the most direct OpenClaw alternative. It provides capabilities OpenClaw lacks: a sandboxed run for every task with nothing on a host of yours, vault-held credentials, per-agent budget enforcement, and a goal-and-task coordination model (goals → tasks → agents). For teams focused on stateful workflow flexibility, LangGraph is another strong alternative. See our full [AI agent frameworks comparison](/learn/ai-agent-frameworks).

### Why choose a managed OpenClaw alternative?

A managed OpenClaw alternative handles the operational security layer that self-hosted OpenClaw deployments require you to build: run isolation, credential vaulting, cost tracking, and multi-channel deployment. OpenLegion provides these as built-in platform features. This removes the DevOps investment needed to move from prototype to production while improving the security posture of your agent team.

### OpenClaw vs OpenLegion: which should I use?

Use OpenClaw if you need a specialized AI coding agent, want the largest open-source community, or prioritize maximum self-hosted flexibility. Use OpenLegion if you need credential isolation (agents never see keys), per-agent budget controls, a structured goal-and-task coordination model, or you're deploying agent teams across customer-facing channels. For a detailed comparison, see [OpenLegion vs OpenClaw](/comparison/openclaw).

### Does OpenLegion require my LLM API keys?

No. Models come with the platform and are chosen by preset — Smartest, Smart or Normal — per agent or per workspace, so there are no provider keys to bring. Work is metered in credits at $0.001 each and the exact cost of each task is visible. Credentials you connect live in a vault and are injected outside the model, which only ever holds a handle. Agents never see raw keys.

### Can I self-host instead of using hosted OpenLegion?

Not at launch. OpenLegion is a hosted web app: sign in with Google and start — there is nothing to install. The separately published engine is source-available under the PolyForm Perimeter License 1.0.1, but the hosted platform is proprietary and has no self-hosted edition. No Redis, no Kubernetes, no infrastructure of your own to run. Free is $0 with 1,000 one-time credits and no card.

### How hard is it to migrate from OpenClaw to OpenLegion?

There is nothing to install, so migration is configuration, not deployment. LLM routing does not transfer: OpenLegion chooses models by preset — Smartest, Smart or Normal. Tool integrations require adaptation to OpenLegion's permission matrix, and you'll describe agent teams to the assistant in the app. Credential migration is a one-time vault configuration. The main trade-off: you gain sandboxed runs, vault-held credentials, and budget controls; you lose OpenClaw's specialized coding capabilities and its large community ecosystem.
